lines: A Bond Crest. On my kitchen table. Well.
Your father got his first one at nineteen and never once shut up about it.
You have until the kettle boils. Then I want all of it.
Let me look at it again. Go on.
It is watching me back. I do not think I will ever get used to that.
Eat something that is not dried fish, {name}. That is the whole of my advice.
There you are. Up before me, which has happened twice in sixteen years.
Professor Sorrell came by at dawn asking for you. At DAWN.
Go on. Over the bridge, the long low one with the charts in the windows.
Wellhead's brim full and it is humming again. Loud enough that Nell can hear it, and Nell hears nothing.
Down to a hand's depth in the spring and full to the lip now, and no rain worth the name up here.
Nobody has told me what that means. I would settle for somebody admitting it means something.
You've been out to the coast. Then you can tell me something.
Wellhead's down to a hand's depth and there's been no drought. Ask anyone.
Something is holding the water somewhere. It isn't holding it here.
A Crest already. Don't tell Ollet, he'll get competitive on Tarin's behalf.
Listen. The well's stopped humming. Three nights now, nothing at all.
I thought that would be a relief. It isn't.
So Sorrell gave you one after all. Look at the size of it.
Do me a favour on your way out. Stand by the well a minute and just listen.
Then come back and tell me I'm not going soft. Nobody else in this town will.
Morning, {name}. Sixteen today and off up that road, I'm told.
I've drawn water out of that wellhead since before your mother moved in.
It hums some nights. Everyone tells me it's the pipes. It isn't the pipes.
There are eleven on Route 1 now and I can name four of them, same four as always.
The new ones came up the road. UP the road, from the coast, which is the wrong way for anything.
I have put them in my book with no names on. It is the worst page in there and it is my favourite.
You've GOT one. Can I see it? Can I hold it? Can I name it?
...Fine. But I'm putting it in my book anyway and I'm spelling it how I like.
I can name every kin on Route 1. Go on, test me.
...I can name four kin on Route 1.
The fifth one just screams and leaves. You try writing that down.
So you're off. Right then, one piece of advice and it's free.
Deep grass is where the kin are and deep grass is where you can't see your feet.
Both of those are true at once. That's the whole job, that is.
Walked the coast road down from Briarbell this morning. Twelve miles, and this is the first water I've seen moving.
Everything else out there is standing still and going green.
Ask your professor about that. Don't ask me, I only walk past it.
Two Crests. He sent a letter about the second one and spent most of it complaining it took three tries.
Not one word about the first. That is how I know which one he is proud of.
He is in Stonewake and he has not been near the Hall. I can hear it in the handwriting.
Something has got hold of him out there. Better it were a Hallkeeper.
If you see him, {name} — do not tell him I asked.
A Crest. My child. There is a letter on that shelf I have read eleven times.
He says he pulled a cart out of a ford. Four lines on the Crest and a page and a half on the cart.
Word came down the road before the letter did. Beat the Briarbell Keeper first ask.
His mother will be unbearable and she is two regions away.
Go and get yours. He will want somebody to measure himself against, and it had better be you.
He is somewhere up past the tarn by now. Sixteen and gone, just like that.
You caught him up, did you? Good. Keep doing that.
Not to beat him, {name}. So he has somebody to be sensible at.
Gone, is he. Didn't take the lunch I packed him either.
His mother keeps a Kin Hall two regions off. He's decided that's a debt.
It isn't. Tell him that somewhere I'm not standing. He might hear it from you.
Tarin hasn't sat down since Sorrell sent word. Wore a line in my floor.
Two starters, two candidates, and my child has decided that's a duel.
Try not to let it be a duel. That's all I'm asking. Try.
So that's what you went with.
Huh. Not what I'd have taken. Which means beating you will actually count.
Don't look at me like that, I'm being nice.
Do not knock. You have never knocked. Do not start today of all days.
Two starters and two candidates in the whole village, {name}, and I have done the maths on that about nine hundred times.
Go and pick. I'll wait. I'm excellent at waiting, ask my father.
You've met Kerrow. I can tell. People go quiet in a particular way afterwards.
She isn't lying to you. That's the difficult part. She never has been.
Keep the Vellum open. Facts first. Sides afterwards, if you must.
Still here? Sit. No, don't, you'll only fidget and I'll watch you do it.
Keep the Vellum open and keep your eyes up.
Anything that is where it shouldn't be, I want to know. Especially the dull ones.
You came. Good. Sit, don't sit, whichever gets you talking faster.
I study movement. Not battling, not breeding. Movement.
And something in the Caeloran Sea is early this year. Decades early.
Mind the charts on your way past. Those pins are older than I am.
He hasn't slept in two days. He says the currents feel wrong.
He's usually right. That's the annoying part.
Go through, he's expecting you. Mind the charts, the pins are ancient.
And if you can get him to eat anything on your way out, I'll owe you.
I've been trying since Tuesday.

r1_walker: Six hours out, six hours back, and one interesting rock to show for it.
Ashgate's north if you stay on the spine road and don't get clever.

lines: You felt it too, then. Ground went quiet about an hour back.
Birds left first. They always do.
Get to Ashgate. Somebody there will want to hear it from you and not me.
Stay out of the deep grass until that one of yours has some weight on it.
Nothing on this route will kill you. Plenty of it will embarrass you.
And watch the pond at dusk. Only at dusk. Don't ask me why, I've stopped asking.
Go and see Sorrell. I'll be right behind you.
Obviously I'll be right behind you. I've been up since four.
My cousin keeps a stall on the Tideglass Parade and she has come home. Walked it.
She will not say much about it. She has never in her life not said much about anything.
So there is one more stall in this square this Tuesday. That is all it looks like from here.
Now don't come to me for vessels, {name}, I sell eggs and rope and bootlaces.
There's a proper Provisioner up the road with a blue roof on it. Ask for the blue roof.
And take a loaf. No. Take it. I have known you since you were a fortnight old.
Four stalls on a Tuesday and two of them are mine, so you can see how the market's going.
Everyone says go where the money is. The money is up the coast and I am not.
Big day for you, I hear. Your mother's told the whole square twice.
One already. I told them. I stood at that board and I told them.
Come here. Nearer. — No, I have nothing to say, I only wanted a proper look at you.
Elias went up that same road at about your age with a bag and no sense at all.
I am not going to tell you to be careful. Nobody ever listened and I would not either.
I will tell you to come back, though. That part is allowed.
Eighty-one years in this village and I have been up that road four times.
Twice for a wedding, once for a funeral, once because I was cross.
You will do better than that by Tuesday.
You have stood at a harbour by now. Do not tell me. I can see you worked out I was right.
The mere has come up over the staithe and the fish are back out in the middle of it, all of them.
One river, one man, my whole life. And I knew. That is not a comfort, {name}. I thought it would be.
Don't fall in on your way past. It would spoil the whole story.
Go on. And when you're somewhere with a harbour, look at the water and tell me what it's doing.
Nobody believes a man who only ever stood in one river.
Mere's running warm. In autumn. It has not run warm in autumn in my lifetime.
The fish know it too. They've all gone up under the far bank and they will not come out.
Your professor keeps writing it down. I keep telling him writing it down is not the same as doing something.
Off, then! Go on, out of my field.
...I do not mean that. Come here. Take a handful of these for the road.
They're only beans. But they are the good ones and I do not give them to just anybody.
Second cut of the year and it should be the last. Look at it. It is still growing.
Everything is early. The hay, the birds, the whole business.
Maben's law: when the ground is early, something is coming that the ground knows about first.
So he's gone. He came in, ate nothing, and hugged me for about a second and a half.
That is a long hug for that boy. Do not tell him I counted.
Look at the pair of you. I have watched you two through that window since you could walk.
You will fight the whole length of this region and you will not mean a word of it.
Go on. And keep an eye on him, {name}. He does not keep one on himself.
That's a nice one. Mind the deep grass down the lower meadow, though.
Something in there put my dog up a tree last week. My dog. Up a tree.
I only come in here for the warm and the keeper knows it.
Nothing wrong with either of mine. Both fifteen years old and both furious about it.
That loud lad off the west road came up out of the mire yesterday and did not say a word.
Walked straight past the Hall. He had a Crest off Tallow only Tuesday and he walked straight past it.
Two of them went out along the sanctum causeway this morning, and one was your friend.
The Foundation have had that place nine days. I would not have gone. He went first.
Everyone on this wharf has heard about the north road by now.
Your friend has not made one joke all morning. That is how I know it was bad.
Your friend took the Channel Crest off Mabry, and he went down the deep lane to do it.
Nobody goes down the deep lane on purpose. He came up laughing.
That loud friend of yours went to hear Dr. Veyl on the wharf and came away very quiet.
Said the man seemed decent and it was bothering him. Strange thing to complain about.
There's a lad been sat on the milestone since dawn with a slate, counting carts.
I asked him why. He said somebody had to, and offered me his tea.
That loud lad took the Stone Crest off the Keeper yesterday. Third go at it.
He told the whole square it was his third go. I did not expect that from him.
There is a boy been sleeping on the Hall steps and he has not once gone inside it.
Spends his days stood outside that grey office instead. Somebody ought to feed him.
A lad hauled Wick's cart clean out of the ford yesterday. One kin and a lot of shouting.
Would not take a coin for it. Would not stop talking about it either.
You have heard, then. The Hallkeeper, first ask, before half this town was up.
He has told me twice and I was standing there.
A boy came through at a dead run about an hour back. Did not stop.
Waved, mind. Ran into a fence doing it.
Ollet's boy went up the north road this morning like the ground was on fire behind him.
Ollet's boy has been stood outside the field station since before it was light.
In this. Would not come in for tea.
Quiet road, this one. Suits me. Does not suit everybody.
Word came down off the north road this morning. The Hall is not saying anything.
We have doubled the lamps on the sea gate, mind. Nobody asked us to.
Three Crests, and he took the deep lane to get the third.
Mabry has not decided whether she is furious. She keeps saying "the deep lane" to herself.
The loud one was in the gallery for the speech. Front row. Did not heckle once.
I had money on him heckling.
Two Crests, and he is spending his week on a hillside watching carts go past.
I have seen worse instincts in Trainers holding eight.
Your friend came back a third time and took it off her.
She said afterwards she had never been so pleased to lose to anybody.
The loud one? He signed the book his first day here and he has not been back to it since.
Signing the book is the easy half. I have told him.
The boy with the one Crest went east into the ruin wood.
Said he was going to catch something impossible. He may well have done.
He beat her before breakfast. I hold the keys to this building and I was not even here yet.
Sign the book. Everybody signs the book, including the ones who never come back.
The loud one came in and asked whether we treat people. Not kin. People.
I said yes. He said good, and went out again. I did not care for that at all.
Three Crests in him now and he still turns up soaked to the collar.
I have started keeping a towel back with his name on it.
He sat in my waiting room for an hour after his kin were done. Just sat.
Then thanked me twice and left.
Young man came down off the ridge with a kin that had been up all night, and no coat.
Ate two bowls of anything I put in front of him. Would not sit down.
Your friend, is he? He carries them in bruised and he is gone before I have finished.
He has been in four times this week and I still do not know his name.
In at seven with a Slatewing and no manners whatsoever. Lovely boy. Filthy.
We put them back together and we do not charge you. That is the whole of it.
Last I heard your friend was somewhere about {tarin_where}, if you were going to ask.
He bought every Dusk Vessel on the shelf and asked what else works after dark.
Sixteen years old, asking me that. In my shop.
Boy with three Crests came in dripping on my floor and bought rope.
Rope. In a Kin shop.
The green-jacket lad bought six storm cards and would not take them for nothing.
Said if they were free then somebody else was paying.
The boy with the tally slate bought a flask, a lamp and nothing whatever to eat.
I have had that customer before. He was sixteen as well.
Cleaned me out of Strong Potions, that one, then came back and apologised for it.
He bought rope. A lot of rope, and he would not say what for.
I have been in this trade thirty years. Rope is never nothing.
Bought three Strong Potions and told me he only needed one. I did not follow the logic either.
Take your time. Nothing on that shelf is going anywhere.
Eleven runs this week, same crates, same hour, and the last four were heavier.
They don't tell us what's in them. I stopped asking, because the money is good and I am not brave.
Contract work. Coast road, dawn till it is done, and they pay the same if it rains.
Best winter my family has had. I am not going to pretend otherwise to be interesting.
Somebody from the office has been down here all morning asking to see the movement orders.
She is very polite about it and she is not going away. I have never seen that before.
You were at the wharf, then. He does that everywhere. Never sends anyone.
Storm cards in the crate. Take two. They cost us nothing and they have cost me nothing but sleep.
Coastal survey. Nothing to look at, and I mean that literally. It is soundings.
There is a crate of storm cards at the tent if you are walking on. They are free, they are always free.
We were on his sea wall until four this morning, laying bags on the top of it.
His wall. The one he would not put his name on. Holding, so far, and everybody saying so.
And he has not come. Every other time, he came. I keep looking down the road for him.
I heard what happened up the north road, and I am not having it laid at his door.
That man rebuilt our sea wall and would not put his name on it. You do not do that and then do this.
He stood on a table in the rain for an hour and answered every question he was asked.
My husband went in to shout at him about the harbour dues. Came out having been agreed with.
Veyl is speaking on the wharf. Actually here, actually himself, which nobody believed.
Half this city owes him a roof and the other half will not say so out loud.

_storm: ACT 5, THE WEATHER. Canon: once Meridian begin waking the ancient systems the weather turns across the whole region and NPC dialogue changes with it. The gate for every one of those variants, in this file and in the ten settlement files, is the flag act4_done -- the one the theft sets as the player walks out of the Aureline square, which is exactly the moment Meridian have the Tideheart and start. No new flag was invented and no engine change was needed: registry.lines already resolves ifFlags, first match wins, so each storm block sits at the TOP of its entry's variant list and the pre-storm lines stay underneath untouched. If a later beat wants a second, worse tier, add a block above the act4_done one on its own flag -- an unset flag simply falls through to this tier, so it degrades safely. RESTRAINT IS THE POINT: roughly two or three people per settlement changed, never a whole town, and several of the strongest lines (Maben's law in Hearthmere, the Tideglass old hand's "busy is what a city looks like just before something happens to it", the Mirehaven harbourmaster telling you not to lean on anything you did not test) were deliberately LEFT ALONE, because they land harder unchanged. Ordering is carried by content rather than by flags: the coast is frightened, the inland towns are puzzled, and Hearthmere hears it from somebody's cousin. Nobody anywhere blames Meridian -- the world notices weather, not a cause.
